subject: Climate & Environment
title: Drought and Food Security
description: A 60-second lesson on Drought and Food Security.

hook.text: The 2011 East Africa drought left 13 million people facing starvation.

buildup.text: Crops failed across Somalia, Kenya, and Ethiopia after two consecutive rainy seasons failed.

discovery.text: When drought kills harvests, food prices spike — hitting the poorest hardest.

twist.text: Climate models predict more frequent droughts in regions that already struggle to feed themselves.

climax.text: Drought-resistant crops and better water storage can buffer the worst impacts.

punchline.text: When the rain fails, hunger follows within weeks.

quiz.question: How many people faced starvation in the 2011 East Africa drought?

details.summary: Drought is the single most damaging natural hazard for agriculture, destroying crops and killing livestock across vast regions. Climate change is increasing drought frequency and severity in key farming areas, threatening food security for hundreds of millions of the world's most vulnerable people.
details.whyItMatters: Food and water crises are deeply linked. Drought-driven crop failures trigger famine, displacement, and conflict, amplifying existing instability in vulnerable regions.
takeaways: Drought is the most damaging natural hazard for agriculture
Climate change increases drought frequency in farming regions
Crop failures from drought trigger famine and displacement

faq.question: Which regions are most at risk of drought-driven famine?
faq.answer: The Horn of Africa, the Sahel, South Asia, and Central America face the highest risks. Consecutive failed rainy seasons in East Africa have pushed tens of millions toward starvation. Smallholder farmers with no irrigation are the most exposed.

faq.question: Can drought-resistant crops reduce the impact?
faq.answer: Drought-tolerant varieties help but are not a complete solution. They need complementary investments in irrigation, soil health, early warning systems, and social safety nets. Diversifying crops and adopting agroecological practices also build resilience.
